title: Test Your Understanding: Design a Payment System
description: Trade-offs and failure modes from the payment system case study.

questions.question: Why do card payment systems separate authorization from capture/settlement?

options.text: To reduce database writes
Authorization reserves funds and validates the card; capture/settlement actually moves money — often batched later
PCI DSS requires two separate servers
So the PSP can charge double fees

questions.explanation: Authorization is fast and reserves funds; settlement moves money and may batch. They can fail independently — your design must track both states.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an append-only ledger vs a mutable wallet?

options.text: Ledger is faster for reads
Wallet holds operational balance; ledger is immutable audit trail for disputes and reconciliation
Wallet is only for customers; ledger is only for merchants
They are interchangeable if you use SQL transactions

questions.explanation: Wallet answers 'how much can I withdraw now?'; ledger answers 'what happened and can finance prove it?' On conflict, rebuild wallet from ledger.

questions.question: A client times out during authorizePayment and retries. What prevents a duplicate authorization hold?

options.text: Disabling all retries
Idempotency key — server returns the same result for the same key
Using GET instead of POST
Caching the response in Redis for 1 second only

questions.explanation: Idempotency keys let the server recognize duplicate intents. Retries are required for reliability; idempotency makes them safe.

questions.question: What does the daily reconciliation job compare?

options.text: Customer passwords across regions
Internal ledger captures vs PSP settlement file
Fraud scores vs marketing campaigns
Load balancer configs in two data centers

questions.explanation: Reconciliation matches your recorded captures to what the PSP actually settled. Mismatches block blind payouts and surface bugs or PSP outages.

questions.question: Why decouple fraud/risk checks from the payment gateway (PSP)?

options.text: PSPs cannot run fraud rules
Independent scaling, faster rule changes, and smaller blast radius on deploys
It eliminates the need for idempotency keys
Card networks require it by law

questions.explanation: Fraud logic changes often and scales differently than PSP I/O. Separation lets you iterate rules without touching PCI-heavy gateway integrations.

questions.question: Authorization succeeded but settlement failed. What should the system expose?

options.text: status = PAID — customer email already sent
Explicit txn states (e.g. AUTHORIZED, CAPTURE_PENDING, SETTLED, FAILED) and reconciliation alerts
Delete the transaction row and ask user to retry
Only log to stdout — finance will figure it out

questions.explanation: Auth success without settlement is a real production scenario. State machine + reconciliation prevents silent money loss.

questions.question: In this design, issuer banks and card networks are considered in-scope components we build and operate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Banks and card networks are external. We orchestrate via PSP APIs and maintain internal wallet, ledger, and reconciliation.
